nodes_source.source_quote: In this work, we propose a deep reinforcement learning (DRL) method to explore the potential of traffic video data in improving the efficiency of ramp metering.
nodes_source.description: High-dimensional visual inputs in the form of preprocessed video data/frames from which vehicle locations are extracted and reformed as position matrices. This data is used as input for the DRL method, for simulation experiments, and to calibrate SUMO driving behaviors.
nodes_source.reproducibility_rationale: The data used to support the results of this study are available from the corresponding author upon request.

nodes_process.node_name: Extract vehicle locations and form position matrices
nodes_process.source_quote: Vehicle locations are extracted from the traffic video frames and are reformed as position matrices.
nodes_process.description: Vehicle locations are extracted from raw traffic video frames and represented as a position matrix. Each vehicle is a location point, and the signal state information is also included in the matrix.
nodes_process.reproducibility_rationale: clarity=2, no specific tools or parameter values stated for location extraction.

nodes_process.node_name: Form traffic state from position matrices
nodes_process.source_quote: Since one matrix is insufficient to describe vehicle dynamics, we stack the matrices of consecutive N time steps to represent the state s_t: S_t = {m_t-(N-1),..., m_t}.
nodes_process.description: Consecutive position matrices from N time steps are stacked to represent the traffic state. Down-sampling is applied before stacking to reduce input dimensions and maintain sufficient information about vehicle positions.
nodes_process.reproducibility_rationale: clarity=3, output dimension implies some parameters, but down-sampling method not explicitly detailed.

nodes_process.source_quote: We adopt a deep neural network termed Q-network to approximate Q* (s, a).
nodes_process.description: A deep Q-learning model is trained using a Q-network with convolutional and fully connected layers. Training employs experience replay, a target network, and a multitask learning strategy to predict speed and queue length alongside Q-values. The Adam optimizer is used.
nodes_process.reproducibility_rationale: clarity=4, Adam optimizer named, 7/9 parameters stated, gamma and total episodes missing.

nodes_process.source_quote: The reward r_t after action a_t is defined by the following: r_t = v_t + wq_t, > 0, w < 0
nodes_process.description: The reward function is defined as a linear combination of the average speed in the merging area (v_t) and the average queue length at the on-ramp (q_t). Positive mu and negative omega are the respective weights.

nodes_process.source_quote: The proposed method is evaluated in SUMO, an open-source microscopic traffic simulator [31].
nodes_process.description: A microscopic traffic simulation environment is set up using SUMO to model a freeway network with an on-ramp and mainline, based on a real-world case study in Qingdao, China. Driving behavior parameters are calibrated using empirical data.
nodes_process.reproducibility_rationale: clarity=3, SUMO mentioned, speed limits and time stated, but driving behavior parameter calibration details missing.

nodes_process.source_quote: The first scenario does not apply ramp metering
nodes_process.description: Traffic flow is simulated in the SUMO environment without any ramp metering control to establish a baseline for comparative analysis. Simulations are initialized with different random seeds.
nodes_process.reproducibility_rationale: clarity=4, SUMO used, random seeds mentioned but specific values not stated.

nodes_process.source_quote: the second scenario adopts the PI-ALINEA method.
nodes_process.description: The PI-ALINEA ramp metering method is simulated, which fixes the green phase length and determines the red phase length based on previous cycle red phase and downstream occupancies. Simulations are initialized with different random seeds.
nodes_process.reproducibility_rationale: clarity=4, SUMO mentioned, PI-ALINEA formula and most parameters stated, random seed values missing.

nodes_process.source_quote: The proposed DRL method results in lower travel times in the mainline
nodes_process.description: The trained DRL model is deployed within the SUMO environment to control ramp metering signals. The traffic system's performance is evaluated. Simulations are initialized with different random seeds.
nodes_process.reproducibility_rationale: clarity=4, SUMO used, decision step size stated, random seeds mentioned but values not stated.

nodes_process.source_quote: Figure 8: Convergence curves for (a) episode reward and (b) mean travel time.
nodes_process.description: The DRL model's training convergence is analyzed by plotting the episode reward and mean travel time over training frames to demonstrate stability and learning progress.
nodes_process.reproducibility_rationale: clarity=4, standard analysis and plotting techniques.

nodes_process.source_quote: Figure 9 presents the Q1, Q2, and Q3 of the travel times in the mainline for three scenarios.
nodes_process.description: Vehicle travel times in the mainline are statistically analyzed using quartiles (Q1, Q2, Q3) for the no-control, PI-ALINEA, and DRL scenarios to compare their impact on traffic flow efficiency. Mean travel times from 20 experiments are also tabulated.
nodes_process.reproducibility_rationale: clarity=4, standard statistical analysis and plotting.

nodes_process.source_quote: Figure 10 presents the temporal-spatial distribution of the mean speeds along the mainline.
nodes_process.description: The mean speeds along the mainline are visualized over time and space for the no-control, PI-ALINEA, and DRL scenarios to assess traffic flow efficiency and congestion patterns.

nodes_process.source_quote: Figure 11 presents the Q1, Q2, and Q3 of the queue lengths at the on-ramp in three scenarios.
nodes_process.description: Queue lengths at the on-ramp are statistically analyzed for the no-control, PI-ALINEA, and DRL scenarios, including quartiles and average values, to compare how each method manages ramp queues.
nodes_process.reproducibility_rationale: clarity=4, standard statistical analysis and plotting.

nodes_process.node_name: Analyze queue length and red ratio relationship
nodes_process.source_quote: Figure 12 presents the mean queue lengths at the on-ramp and the red ratios (i.e., the proportion of the red phase in the simulation time) in each simulation for the two ramp metering methods.
nodes_process.description: The relationship between mean queue lengths at the on-ramp and the red ratio (proportion of red phase) is analyzed for PI-ALINEA and DRL methods to understand metering rate impacts on queue formation.
nodes_process.reproducibility_rationale: clarity=4, standard statistical analysis and plotting.

nodes_process.source_quote: Figure 13 presents the queue lengths at the on-ramp and the occupancy downstream of the merging area for the two ramp metering methods.
nodes_process.description: The temporal evolution of queue lengths at the on-ramp and occupancy downstream of the merging area are analyzed for PI-ALINEA and DRL methods, including their correlation, to assess system dynamics.
nodes_process.reproducibility_rationale: clarity=4, standard statistical analysis and plotting.

nodes_process.source_quote: The better performance of the proposed DRL method is further revealed when considering traffic flows downstream of the merge area, which is demonstrated in Figure 14.
nodes_process.description: Traffic flows downstream of the merge area are compared across the no-control, PI-ALINEA, and DRL scenarios to evaluate the impact on throughput and alleviation of capacity drop impacts.
nodes_process.reproducibility_rationale: clarity=4, standard traffic analysis and plotting.

nodes_process.source_quote: A perturbation analysis is conducted to evaluate the impact of information contained in video data.
nodes_process.description: The control area is divided into eight subareas. Information from each subarea is systematically removed from the original data to create perturbed datasets for subsequent simulations.
nodes_process.reproducibility_rationale: clarity=3, number of subareas mentioned but exact perturbation mechanism not fully detailed.

nodes_process.source_quote: Figure 16 presents the box plot of travel time when the information of different subareas is removed, and the baseline is the result of experiments that take original data as input.
nodes_process.description: DRL ramp metering simulations are run using the perturbed input data sets, and the resulting travel times are collected for comparison against a baseline using original data. Twenty experiments are conducted per subarea.
nodes_process.reproducibility_rationale: clarity=4, SUMO used, number of experiments stated, random seeds mentioned but values not stated.

nodes_process.node_name: Evaluate travel time with perturbed data
nodes_process.source_quote: Figure 16 presents the box plot of travel time when the information of different subareas is removed, and the baseline is the result of experiments that take original data as input.
nodes_process.description: Travel times from simulations with perturbed input data are visualized using box plots. This analysis shows the impact of missing information from different subareas on the DRL method's performance.
nodes_process.reproducibility_rationale: clarity=4, standard statistical analysis and plotting.
